title.narrative: Coastal Region Water Security and Climate Resilience Project

description.narrative: The development objective of this project (KWSCRP-2) is to increase bulk water supply to Mombasa County and Kwale County, and increase access to water in Kwale County.

The objective of the Coastal Region Water Security and Climate Resilience Project for Kenya is to sustainably increase bulk water supply to Mombasa County and Kwale County, and increase access to water and sanitation in Kwale County. The project has three components. (1) Mwache Dam and related infrastructure component will finance the construction of the main dam (Mwache), one check dam, raw water transmission lines (gravity-fed) to the treatment plant, and transport infrastructure (approach road to dam site and bridges), as well as supply electromechanical equipment and buildings related to the dam site to the water supply system in the coastal region. (2) Kwale county development component will support development in Kwale County, where the Mwache Dam is located, through investments in water supply and sanitation in rural communities and small towns; a demonstration irrigation scheme to inform, design, and establish the viability of a large scale irrigation program in Kwale in the future; and livelihoods investments support. (3) Project management component will finance the required office space, goods, equipment, staff, consultant services, travel, training, and operating costs that will allow for the successful implementation of project activities. These responsibilities include project management and coordination, procurement and financial management, project monitoring and evaluation, social and environmental safeguards management and oversight, and strategic project communications and outreach.

title.narrative: Target land area under sustainable land and water management practices

comment.narrative: Definition Enhanced - The indicator measures, in hectares, the land area for which sustainable land and water management (SLWM) practices have been introduced. SLWM practices refer to a combination of technologies or practices (agronomic, vegetative, structural, and management measures) applied to improve land quality and prevent degradation or restore already degraded landscape. These include physical soil and water conservation techniques (e.g., marker and contour ridges, terracing, box ridges, water harvesting, infiltration ditches, gully reclamation, etc); vegetative river/stream bank restoration; agricultural technologies (i.e. agroforestry and farmer-managed natural regeneration), afforestation and reforestation, community/individual woodlots, etc

title.narrative: Number of people provided with basic access to water

comment.narrative: This indicator measures the total number of people in drought-vulnerable project areas in Kwale county gaining access to improved drinking water sources as a result of project interventions. An improved drinking water source means any of the following sources: piped household connections (house or yard connections), public standpipe, boreholes, water-kiosks, protected dug well, protected spring, and rainwater collection. Water for productive use meanns using water for irrigation,livestock, fisheries, and water for small-scale processing. Access means water is either delivered at the point of production or is within 250m from the point of production

title.narrative: Bulk water supply from Mwache Dam

comment.narrative: The civil works and associated programs have progressed well this period and impounding of the main dam is schehduled to start in 2026. The time Elapsed as at 15th August 2025 is 40.5 months (75%) of the Contract period while the progress of permanent works stands at 46.0% complete. The lower check dam and access roads performed relatively well, nearing their respective targets. Therefore since the last mission, a 17.9% points progress has been registered.

title.narrative: Number of public schools provided with WASH facilities under the project

comment.narrative: During this period, infrastructure in two (2) more schools ( Mlola and Chidzipwa - Lot I) were completed contributing an additional 259 (120 B, 139G).

title.narrative: Target land area under sustainable land and water management practices

comment.narrative: Since March 2025, the project put an additional 68.4 ha of land under sustainable management. Therefore in 12 months, between July 2024 & June 2025, the project achieved significant milestones with a total of 230.9ha restored. This includes 54.18 km of terraces excavated across six sub-catchments, conserving over 162 hectares of land. Gabion construction reached 1,208 meters, stabilizing gullies and protecting an additional 24 hectares. Vetiver bulking sites were established in four sub-catchments, providing a sustainable source of vegetative material for bioengineering. Rainwater harvesting tanks were installed in nine WRUAs, improving water access for schools & communities. Riparian marking & pegging was undertaken along 14 km of the Mwadudua River, with 2,000 indigenous trees planted to restore riverine ecology. Additionally, 25,000 mango seedlings were distributed to WRUAs for planting in terraced areas and public institutions. conservation of 606.66 hectares since the last mission

title.narrative: Number of Villages Certified by third party to be Open Defecation Free (ODF)

comment.narrative: Between March and August 2025, the Mwache Dam Project advanced ODF efforts in 15 villages through sanitation campaigns and infrastructure upgrades. Six school sanitation blocks were completed, with three more due in August 2025. These initiatives improved hygiene awareness, reinforced dignity, and laid the groundwork for future ODF certification.

title.narrative: Environmental and Social Management Plan Implemented

comment.narrative: This is a continous qualitative indicator. Between March and August 2025, the Mwache Dam Project advanced its Environmental, Social, Health, and Safety (ESHS) safeguards. Key achievements included finalizing the Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan, resolving blasting-related grievances, and improving site safety through fencing and signage. HIV awareness was strengthened via community health promoters, while local labor sourcing remained high. However, female workforce participation in civil works stayed low. Continued focus on risk mitigation and inclusive engagement remains essential for sustained progress

title.narrative: Cost performance index for Mwache dam and associated works

comment.narrative:
Indicator revised: The end target date has been revised to align with the new project closing date of November 2028.
clarification - Evaluates the ratio of the value of completed work to the actual costs incurred during implementation of the dam and its related infrastructure. A value above 1.0 indicates cost efficiency (more value delivered per unit of expenditure), while a value below 1.0 signals cost overruns. This metric supports financial accountability and timely corrective action.
The cost performance index (CPI) is the ratio of the actual work completed (measured by its earned value) to the actual cost incurred

Details Total in KES % Contract Amount 13,752,164,239.96 100.00% Total Amount Certified 8,179,164,319.84 59.48% Total Amount Disbursed 7,464,069,382.96 54.28% Total Amount Outstanding 715,094,936.88 5.20%
The Cost performance index (CPI) has improved from 0.94 to 1.10 this period. A CPI of 1.096 indicates that the project is performing cost-efficiently. In other words, for every KES 1 spent, the project is delivering approximately KES 1.10 worth of certified work. This is a strong indicator of budget discipline and value-for-money execution.

title.narrative: Schedule performance index of the Mwache dam and associated works

comment.narrative:
As of August 15, 2025, 40.5 months (75%) of the Contract period had elapsed whilst the progress of Permanent works stands at 46.0% complete.
Although there has been progress in works, the current Schedule Performance Index (SPI) of 0.614 for the Mwache Dam and its associated works indicates that the project is significantly behind schedule. This low SPI suggests a high risk of slippage in critical milestones which could affect the timely delivery of key components.Extended timelines may increase overhead costsand hence the need for additional financing It's essential for the government to reassess the cost-to-completion estimates and revise cash flow projections to reflect the current pace of execution.
